etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin cōmoedia +‎ -an, perhaps modelled on Middle French comédien. By surface analysis, comedy +‎ -an.

definitions.definition: An entertainer who performs in a humorous manner, especially by telling jokes.
(by extension) Any person who is humorous or amusing, either characteristically or on a particular occasion.
(dated) A person who performs in theatrical plays.

quote.citation: c. 1606–1607 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Anthonie and Cleopatra”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii]:
quote.text: […]  the quick comediansExtemporally will stage us, and presentOur Alexandrian revels;

quote.citation: 1714, Susanna Centlivre, The Wonder, London: E. Curll and A. Bettesworth, Preface,[1]
quote.text: I Don’t pretend to write a Preface, either to point out the Beauties, or to excuse the Errors, a judicious Reader may possibly discover in the following Scenes, but to give those excellent Comedians their Due, to whom, in some Measure the best Dramatick Writers are oblig’d.

quote.citation: 1755, George Colman, The Connaisseur‎[2], volume 1, London: R. Baldwin, page 1:
quote.text: When a Comedian, celebrated for his excellence in the part of Shylock, first undertook that character, he made daily visits to the center of business, the ’Change, and the adjacent Coffee-houses; that by a frequent intercourse and conversation with “the unforeskinn’d race,” he might habituate himself to their air and deportment.

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 51, in Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: Becky, the nightingale, took the flowers which he threw to her and pressed them to her heart with the air of a consummate comedian.

quote.citation: a. 1587 (date written), Phillip Sidney [i.e., Philip Sidney], An Apologie for Poetrie. […], London:  […]  [James Roberts] for Henry Olney, […], published 1595, →OCLC; republished as Edward Arber, editor, An Apologie for Poetrie (English Reprints), London: [Alexander Murray & Son], 1 April 1868, →OCLC, pages 44–45:
quote.text: This doth the Comedy handle ſo in our priuate and domeſtical matters, as with hearing it, we get as it were an experience, what is to be looked for of a nigardly Demea: of a crafty Danus: of a flattering Gnato: of a vaine glorious Thraſo: and not onely to know what effects are to be expected, but to know who be ſuch, by the ſignifying badge giuen them by the Comedian.

quote.citation: 1644, John Milton, Areopagitica; a Speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc’d Printing, to the Parlament of England, London: [s.n.], →OCLC, page 5:
quote.text: Neither is it recorded that the writings of those old Comedians were supprest, though the acting of them were forbid;

quote.citation: 1783, Hugh Blair, Lectures on Rhetoric and Belles Lettres, London: Whitestone et al., Volume 3, Lecture 47, p. 377,[3]
quote.text: […]  the Dramatic Author, in whom the French glory most, and whom they justly place at the head of all their Comedians, is, the famous Moliere.
